name: Adversarial Machine Learning
description: Adversarial examples, poisoning, backdoors, evasion, and robustness of ML models.

ccs.narrative:
Research on machine learning and security at CCS began taking shape around 2018, with early work concentrating on adversarial attacks, model robustness, and security of ML systems. Adversarial Sensor Attack on LiDAR-based Perception in Autonomous Driving (CCS 2019) set an influential baseline by showing how to Demonstrates spoofing LiDAR sensor inputs to inject fake obstacles, fooling autonomous-vehicle perception models. Parallel contributions—Deep Fingerprinting: Undermining Website Fingerprinting Defenses with Deep Learning (2018) and Property Inference Attacks on Fully Connected Neural Networks using Permutation Invariant Representations (2018) —reinforced the foundational challenges in this space.

A productive wave of CCS work from 2020–2022 deepened the area. Composite Backdoor Attack for Deep Neural Network by Mixing Existing Benign Features (CCS 2020) advanced the field by demonstrating Proposes a stealthy DNN backdoor triggered by mixing existing benign features rather than an obvious patch trigger. Other strong contributions included Realtime Robust Malicious Traffic Detection via Frequency Domain Analysis (2021), Enhancing State-of-the-art Classifiers with API Semantics to Detect Evolved Android Malware (2020), broadening the space of techniques and targets.

The most recent CCS contributions (from 2023 onward) reflect a maturing field that pushes into harder targets and broader threat models. Narcissus: A Practical Clean-Label Backdoor Attack with Limited Information (CCS 2023) exemplified this trend by tackling Presents a practical clean-label backdoor attack succeeding with limited information while evading human inspection. Similarly, Large Language Models for Code: Security Hardening and Adversarial Testing (2023) and DE-FAKE: Detection and Attribution of Fake Images Generated by Text-to-Image Generation Models (2023) show how the community continues to scale and adapt its methods.

uss.narrative:
The earliest papers in this list, all from USENIX Security 2018, show a field still mapping out the basic shape of the threat. Several works asked how machine learning could be attacked or formally trusted: "When Does Machine Learning FAIL? Generalized Transferability for Evasion and Poisoning Attacks" (USENIX 2018) unified evasion and poisoning under a single transferability framework, while "Formal Security Analysis of Neural Networks using Symbolic Intervals" (USENIX 2018) pushed in the opposite direction, trying to prove robustness guarantees rather than just demonstrate breakage. At the same time, attacks were already leaving the image domain and hitting real systems, from speech ("CommanderSong: A Systematic Approach for Practical Adversarial Voice Recognition", USENIX 2018) to transfer-learning pipelines ("With Great Training Comes Great Vulnerability: Practical Attacks against Transfer Learning", USENIX 2018). A notable inversion of the threat model also appeared early: "Turning Your Weakness Into a Strength: Watermarking Deep Neural Networks by Backdooring" (USENIX 2018) repurposed backdoors as a defensive ownership tool.

The 2019-2020 period marks a shift from digital perturbations to the physical and hardware substrate of ML systems. "Terminal Brain Damage" (USENIX 2019) and "DeepHammer" (USENIX 2020) showed that flipping a handful of bits in memory via Rowhammer could destroy a network's accuracy, attacking the model where it actually runs rather than at its input. In parallel, attacks moved into the physical sensing pipeline: "Seeing is Not Believing: Camouflage Attacks on Image Scaling Algorithms" (USENIX 2019) exploited preprocessing, and "Towards Robust LiDAR-based Perception in Autonomous Driving" (USENIX 2020) demonstrated black-box sensor spoofing against self-driving perception. This era also reframed adversarial techniques as protective tools for ordinary users, most prominently "Fawkes: Protecting Privacy against Unauthorized Deep Learning Models" (USENIX 2020), which cloaked photos to defeat facial recognition scrapers.

By 2021-2022 the community converged on backdoor and poisoning attacks as a central, deployment-relevant concern, especially in pipelines that ingest untrusted data. "Explanation-Guided Backdoor Poisoning Attacks Against Malware Classifiers" (USENIX 2021) used model explanations to craft stealthy poison in crowdsourced threat feeds, and the threat broadened beyond images into text ("T-Miner", USENIX 2021; "Hidden Trigger Backdoor Attack on NLP Models via Linguistic Style Manipulation", USENIX 2022) and into distributed training ("FLAME: Taming Backdoors in Federated Learning", USENIX 2022). Defenses matured alongside, with work like "CADE: Detecting and Explaining Concept Drift Samples for Security Applications" (USENIX 2021) tackling the drift that makes security classifiers brittle over time.

Most recently, attention has tracked the rise of generative models and large language models. "Extracting Training Data from Diffusion Models" (USENIX 2023) showed that image generators memorize and leak their training data, while "Glaze: Protecting Artists from Style Mimicry by Text-to-Image Models" (USENIX 2023) again turned adversarial perturbations into a protective shield, this time for artists rather than faces, echoing Fawkes years earlier. The frontier has now reached LLM safety directly, with "Making Them Ask and Answer: Jailbreaking Large Language Models in Few Queries via Disguise and Reconstruction" (USENIX 2024) demonstrating efficient query-based jailbreaks. Across six years the area has moved from proving and breaking image classifiers toward securing the full lifecycle of generative and foundation models.

top4.narrative:
The earliest papers in this list, from 2018, established the core threat surface of adversarial machine learning across security venues. Two themes dominated. First, the discovery that shared, pre-trained models could be weaponized: "Trojaning Attack on Neural Networks" (NDSS 2018) showed an attacker could implant hidden triggers into a network, while "Manipulating Machine Learning: Poisoning Attacks and Countermeasures for Regression Learning" (S&P 2018) formalized training-time poisoning. Second, a defensive countercurrent emerged that tried to put guarantees under these brittle models, with "AI2: Safety and Robustness Certification of Neural Networks with Abstract Interpretation" (S&P 2018) and "Formal Security Analysis of Neural Networks using Symbolic Intervals" (USENIX 2018) bringing program-analysis tools to certify robustness. The same year also broadened the attack catalog beyond images, into voice ("CommanderSong", USENIX 2018), website fingerprinting ("Deep Fingerprinting", CCS 2018), and model/privacy theft ("Stealing Hyperparameters in Machine Learning", S&P 2018).

A clear shift toward backdoors and detection happened in 2019. "Neural Cleanse: Identifying and Mitigating Backdoor Attacks in Neural Networks" (S&P 2019) became the reference point for reverse-engineering hidden triggers, complemented by "ABS: Scanning Neural Networks for Back-doors by Artificial Brain Stimulation" (CCS 2019) and stealthier variants like "Latent Backdoor Attacks on Deep Neural Networks" (CCS 2019). At the same time, certified defenses matured beyond abstract interpretation into randomized smoothing via "Certified Robustness to Adversarial Examples with Differential Privacy" (S&P 2019). A second important move was attacks leaving the digital domain: "Adversarial Sensor Attack on LiDAR-based Perception in Autonomous Driving" (CCS 2019) opened a long line of physical-world autonomous-vehicle work, continued in "Towards Robust LiDAR-based Perception" (USENIX 2020) and "Invisible for both Camera and LiDAR" (S&P 2021). Researchers also noticed the attack-defense arms race feeding back on itself, with "Privacy Risks of Securing Machine Learning Models against Adversarial Examples" (CCS 2019) showing robustness can worsen privacy leakage.

From 2020 the field grew more rigorous and more practical. "HopSkipJumpAttack" (S&P 2020) made decision-based black-box attacks query-efficient, and "Intriguing Properties of Adversarial ML Attacks in the Problem Space" (S&P 2020) pushed the community to reason about realizable objects rather than abstract perturbations. Federated learning became a major battleground, with "Manipulating the Byzantine: Optimizing Model Poisoning Attacks and Defenses for Federated Learning" (NDSS 2021) and "FLAME: Taming Backdoors in Federated Learning" (USENIX 2022), followed by a sobering reality check in "Back to the Drawing Board: A Critical Evaluation of Poisoning Attacks on Production Federated Learning" (S&P 2022), which questioned whether these attacks matter in deployment.

Most recently, the center of gravity moved to large generative models and web-scale training. "Extracting Training Data from Diffusion Models" (USENIX 2023) showed that generative models memorize and leak their training images, while "Glaze: Protecting Artists from Style Mimicry" (USENIX 2023) turned adversarial perturbations into a protective tool for human creators, echoing the earlier privacy-shield idea of "Fawkes" (USENIX 2020). "Poisoning Web-Scale Training Datasets is Practical" (S&P 2024) closed the loop by demonstrating that the foundational assumption of clean internet-scraped data is itself vulnerable. Across these venues the area has evolved from proof-of-concept attacks on single classifiers to a mature discipline spanning certified defenses, physical-world and federated settings, and the privacy and integrity of today's largest generative systems.
